title: South Asians Face Elevated Heart Risk by Age 45 Despite Healthier Habits — and the Paradox Runs Deeper Than Diet
excerpt: A landmark US study of 2,700 adults finds that South Asian Americans have nearly eight times the prediabetes rate of white peers by midlife — even with better diets and less alcohol. The risk may start at birth.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • South Asian Americans face significantly higher prediabetes rates by age 45 compared to other ethnic groups.
  • Despite healthier diets and lower alcohol consumption, South Asians have elevated cardiovascular risks.
  • Genetics and body composition may explain the early onset of health issues in South Asians.
  • Early screening for cardiovascular risks is crucial for South Asian adults.
  • Culturally tailored health interventions are needed for effective prevention.

A landmark study tracking 2,700 adults across two long-running US cohort studies has revealed a troubling paradox: South Asian Americans develop cardiovascular risk factors far earlier than every other major ethnic group in the country — despite reporting healthier diets, lower alcohol consumption and comparable exercise habits.

The research, published in the *Journal of the American Heart Association*, combined data from the Mediators of Atherosclerosis in South Asians Living in America (MASALA) study and the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA), which together followed white, Black, Hispanic, Chinese and South Asian participants aged 45–55 for over a decade.

The Numbers Are Stark

By age 45, nearly one in three South Asian men (30.7%) already had prediabetes — almost eight times the rate among white men (3.9%) and roughly triple the rate among Black (10.4%) and Hispanic men (10.5%). South Asian women showed a similarly outsized gap: 17.6% had prediabetes at 45, compared with 5.7% of white women and 5.1% of Hispanic women.

High blood pressure was also significantly more prevalent among South Asian men (25.5%) compared to white (18.4%), Chinese (6.6%) and Hispanic men (10.1%). By age 55, both South Asian men and women were at least twice as likely to develop type 2 diabetes as their white peers.

Perhaps most confounding: South Asian participants scored the highest diet quality of all racial and ethnic groups studied, drank less alcohol and exercised at comparable levels.

"We're Missing Something Fundamental"

"The mismatch between healthier lifestyle behaviors and clinical risk was surprising," said Dr Namratha Kandula, senior study author and professor of internal medicine and epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine. "This paradox tells us we're missing something fundamental to what is driving this elevated risk among South Asians."

Kandula, who co-founded the MASALA study — the largest longitudinal study of cardiovascular health in South Asian Americans — said the research answers a question physicians have asked for decades: when exactly does the risk begin?

"We've now identified a critical window in the 40s when risk is already high, but disease is still preventable," she said.

Why Genetics and Body Composition May Explain the Gap

Researchers believe that genetics and the so-called "thin-fat" phenotype — a tendency among South Asians to carry more visceral (abdominal) fat despite a lower overall body mass index — may be central to the paradox. Visceral fat is metabolically active and strongly linked to insulin resistance, a precursor to both diabetes and heart disease.

A separate 2023 scientific statement from the American Heart Association noted that South Asian adults face "disproportionately high risk" for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and recommended dietary modifications including increasing whole-grain intake, choosing cooking oils lower in saturated fat and reducing deep-fried preparation methods.

Earlier research from the South Asian Birth Cohort (START) study at McMaster University found that these metabolic differences may begin at birth: South Asian newborns, though smaller overall, had more adipose tissue and higher waist circumference than white newborns — a finding that suggests the risk may be partly intergenerational.

What NRIs and Diaspora Indians Should Do

The findings carry urgent implications for the estimated 5.4 million Indian Americans and the broader South Asian diaspora in the US, UK and Canada.

"If you are a South Asian adult, maintain a healthy lifestyle and get screened sooner — check blood pressure, glucose/A1c levels and cholesterol in early adulthood rather than waiting for symptoms," Kandula advised.

The study highlights the need for:

  • **Earlier screening**: Cardiovascular risk assessment starting in the early 40s, not the standard mid-50s threshold used for other populations
  • **Culturally tailored prevention**: Standard dietary advice may not be sufficient; interventions need to account for South Asian cooking methods, carbohydrate-heavy staples and genetic predisposition
  • **Awareness of the thin-fat paradox**: A "normal" BMI does not mean a South Asian individual is at low cardiovascular risk — waist circumference and visceral fat measurement are more telling markers
Key Recommendations for South Asians
›Start cardiovascular risk assessment in early 40s.
›Implement culturally tailored dietary interventions.
›Monitor waist circumference and visceral fat.

The study's limitations include reliance on self-reported behaviours and the higher socioeconomic status of both the MASALA and MESA participants, which may limit generalisability. The decade-long gap between baseline exams in the two cohorts is also a factor.But the core finding is clear: for South Asian Americans, the clock starts ticking earlier — and conventional wisdom about what constitutes a "healthy" lifestyle may not be protective enough.
